slides.title: Malware and Physical Attacks
points: Recognize malware and physical attacks from their behavior and observable indicators.
Security+ Objective 2.4: given a scenario, analyze indicators of malicious activity.

slides.title: Ransomware
slides.teach: Malware that encrypts or blocks access to data or systems and demands payment or another concession.

course.learn: Malware that encrypts or blocks access to data or systems and demands payment or another concession.

breakdown.explanation: It locks you out and demands something.
Encrypted files, Ransom note, Systems inaccessible

course.why: It targets availability and often adds extortion pressure.
course.example: Shared files are renamed and a payment demand appears.
course.check_q: Which malware typically makes data inaccessible and demands payment?

slides.title: Trojan
slides.teach: Malware disguised as legitimate software or embedded in something that appears useful.

course.learn: Malware disguised as legitimate software or embedded in something that appears useful.

breakdown.explanation: It looks safe or useful, but contains malicious code.

course.why: Users may willingly execute it because it appears legitimate.
course.example: A fake PDF reader installs malware.
course.check_q: Which malware disguises itself as legitimate software?

slides.title: Worm
slides.teach: Self-replicating malware that spreads automatically across systems or networks.

course.learn: Self-replicating malware that spreads automatically across systems or networks.
course.why: It can infect many systems quickly.
course.example: Hosts become infected across the subnet without users opening files.

slides.title: Spyware
slides.teach: Software that secretly monitors activity or collects information.

course.learn: Software that secretly monitors activity or collects information.

breakdown.explanation: It quietly watches and gathers data.

course.why: It can expose sensitive activity and credentials.
course.example: A hidden app records browsing and sends data externally.

slides.title: Bloatware
slides.teach: Unwanted or unnecessary preinstalled software that consumes resources and may increase attack surface.

course.learn: Unwanted or unnecessary preinstalled software that consumes resources and may increase attack surface.

breakdown.explanation: Extra software you do not need.

course.why: More unnecessary software means more resource use and potential vulnerabilities.
course.example: A new laptop includes many unnecessary trial apps.
course.check_q: Which term describes unnecessary preinstalled software?

slides.title: Virus
slides.teach: Malware that attaches to a host file or program and typically requires execution to activate or spread.

course.learn: Malware that attaches to a host file or program and typically requires execution to activate or spread.

breakdown.explanation: It infects another file or program.

course.why: Viruses rely on host content and execution to spread.
course.example: A malicious macro spreads when users open the document.
course.check_q: Which malware typically attaches to a host file?

slides.title: Keylogger
slides.teach: Software or hardware that records keystrokes.

course.learn: Software or hardware that records keystrokes.

breakdown.explanation: It records what a user types.

course.why: Keystrokes can reveal passwords and sensitive data.
course.example: Passwords are stolen immediately after users type them.

slides.title: Logic Bomb
slides.teach: Malicious code that activates when a specific condition or time is met.

course.learn: Malicious code that activates when a specific condition or time is met.

breakdown.explanation: Deletes files on a date, Triggers after account removal

course.why: It can remain dormant until a chosen event occurs.
course.example: Files are deleted when a former employee's account is disabled.
course.exam: Runs only after condition/date → LOGIC BOMB.
course.check_q: Which malware waits for a condition before activating?

slides.title: Rootkit
slides.teach: Malware designed to maintain privileged, hidden access and conceal malicious activity.

course.learn: Malware designed to maintain privileged, hidden access and conceal malicious activity.

breakdown.explanation: It hides deep in the system while keeping powerful access.

course.why: Rootkits make detection and removal difficult.
course.example: Security tools cannot see a malicious kernel module.

slides.title: Physical Brute Force
slides.teach: A physical attack that uses force to bypass locks, barriers, or access controls.

course.learn: A physical attack that uses force to bypass locks, barriers, or access controls.
course.why: Physical controls can be overcome directly.
course.example: An intruder breaks a lock to enter a server room.
course.exam: Force the barrier → PHYSICAL BRUTE FORCE.
course.check_q: Which physical attack uses direct force?

slides.title: RFID Cloning
slides.teach: Copying data from an RFID credential to create a duplicate credential.

course.learn: Copying data from an RFID credential to create a duplicate credential.
course.why: A cloned credential may be accepted as legitimate.
course.example: Two access badges appear to use the same identifier.
course.check_q: Which attack duplicates an RFID credential?

slides.title: Environmental Attack
slides.teach: Using or exploiting environmental conditions to damage systems or affect availability.

course.learn: Using or exploiting environmental conditions to damage systems or affect availability.

breakdown.explanation: The attack uses heat, water, power, or another environmental factor.

course.why: Environmental conditions can disrupt or destroy infrastructure.
course.example: An attacker disables cooling to overheat equipment.
course.exam: Heat/water/power used to cause damage → ENVIRONMENTAL.
course.check_q: Which physical attack targets environmental conditions?

blocks.title: Identify the behavior before naming the attack
items: The key clue is loss of access paired with extortion.
Example: Shared files are encrypted and a payment note appears.
The malware is disguised as something useful.
Example: A fake PDF reader installs malware.
Example: Hosts become infected across the subnet.
Example: Passwords are stolen after users type them.
The code waits for a condition.
Example: Files are deleted when an account is disabled.
The malware focuses on concealment and deep access.
Example: A kernel module is hidden from security tools.
blocks.example: Memory: Ransomware locks · Trojan disguises · Worm spreads · Virus attaches · Keylogger records · Logic bomb triggers · Rootkit hides.

questions.q: Shared files become encrypted and a ransom note appears. Which malware attack is most likely?
questions.explanation: Ransomware makes data inaccessible and adds an extortion demand.

questions.q: A fake utility appears legitimate but installs malware. Which malware type best fits?
questions.explanation: A Trojan disguises malicious code as legitimate software.

questions.q: Malware rapidly spreads across systems without user action. Which type is most likely?
A malicious macro infects documents when users open them. Which type is most likely?
questions.explanation: A virus attaches to a host file or program.

questions.q: Software records every keystroke users type. Which malware is this?
Malicious code waits until a certain date before deleting files. Which attack is this?
questions.explanation: A logic bomb activates on a condition or trigger.

questions.q: A malicious kernel module hides itself while maintaining administrator-level persistence. Which malware is this?
An attacker duplicates an employee access badge and uses the copy successfully. Which physical attack is this?
questions.explanation: RFID cloning copies credential data from the original badge.
